citations.sentence: Kairos, a chatbot from the ministry Transform Iran, is an AI tool that answers questions about Christianity [[1]].
Transform Iran's Lana Silk told Mission Network News (MNN) how people are using it, in comments MNN reported Sep 24 [[1]].
Kairos is not new; MNN described it as "newly launched" in August 2025 [[2]].
**How it works, according to Transform Iran.** Kairos answers from a closed library rather than the open web [[2]] [[3]].
**How it works, according to Transform Iran.** Kairos answers from a closed library rather than the open web [[2]] [[3]].
The ministry says "every response is carefully curated from Scripture and strictly vetted resources" [[4]].
A December 2025 Transform Iran newsroom post about a KMUZ Radio interview described its knowledge base as "over 5,000 articles, apologetics, and Scripture" [[3]].
A Transform Iran statement to The Christian Post in August cited "nearly 7,000 research articles" from its Porpasokh Apologetics Center [[5]].
When Kairos is unsure, it is designed to say, "I do not know the answer to your question" [[3]].
Transform Iran says questions beyond its database are "flagged for human review and answered within 48 hours" [[4]].
It changed Kairos' wording after the tool began offering to pray for people, so users understood it "guides them in prayer, rather than replacing the role of God or a human pastor" [[3]].
Transform Iran provides a free VPN, a service that hides a user's internet traffic, "to keep their spiritual inquiries safe" [[1]].
Transform Iran says "every response is monitored by Christian theologians and apologists" [[4]].
MNN describes the service as strictly anonymous unless a user chooses to say who they are [[1]].

Transform Iran reports that a man it calls "Keyvan," a pseudonym, contacted Kairos in January, prayed as guided, and "reached out to a church community recommended by Kairos" [[6]].
Silk also told The Christian Post about a man who said, "I've chosen to follow Jesus" [[5]].
Transform Iran says Silk has welcomed scrutiny from YouVersion founder Bobby Gruenewald [[3]].
The ministry is also plain about the tool's limits: "It is not a replacement for faith, discernment, or pastoral care" [[4]].
**Music Bible launches its app.** A team led by founder Micah Fiechter has used AI to set the entire Bible to music in 11 genres, plus three in Spanish [[7]].
The Music Bible app (themusicbible.org) launched Sep 22 on iOS and Android [[8]].

The company says it uses AI tools including Suno and ChatGPT for the music, never to interpret Scripture, though its own page notes that "occasionally, a word or phrase may be repeated for musical expression" [[9]].
Human reviewers check the songs, and Fiechter says flagged ones are pulled "within 24 hours" [[10]].
"I personally, at this moment in time, do not support the use of AI for interpreting Scripture," he said [[10]].

In an NPR/Ipsos poll of 1,011 adults, published by NPR on Sep 25 and updated Sep 28, 11% of AI users surveyed said they have sought spiritual guidance from AI, 13% have used it to generate prayers and 15% to study Scripture [[11]].
Nearly 7 in 10 AI users surveyed said they would never seek spiritual guidance from AI, and just 6% of all adults surveyed currently do [[11]].

YouVersion's Bobby Gruenewald says even the best AI models misquote Scripture at least 15% of the time, and YouVersion has chosen not to launch a public-facing chatbot that answers theological questions [[12]].
He was describing open-ended AI chat models, not Kairos, but the standard is a fair one to apply: "we need it to be better in order to rely on it" [[12]].
